summary:
This project addresses the harmonization of historical fire data by developing a web application that unifies and harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensor records into a single burning activity calendar. 
The main objective is to provide scientists, brigade members and land administrators with a consistent vision that allows them to anticipate critical periods and coordinate the response to fire.
 In addition, it was proposed to resolve the lack of communication among brigade members in remote areas through the deployment of secure networks with LoRa technology (Meshtastic + ATAK).

Key results include the successful development of the web platform with two functional modules (an interactive map for temporal analysis/data download and an emergency management tool), along with robust fire hazard index (FWI) integration. This system was successfully validated through a pilot test that collected and analyzed 20 years of historical records in the town of Carpintería, San Luis (Argentina), using critical meteorological and vegetation cover variables to consolidate the accuracy of the model.
details:
Challenge Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS hot spots

The present challenge is about understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, allowing us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.

Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is broken up across sensors whose data cannot be directly compared, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred.

For active fires, detection and monitoring rely primarily on mid-infrared (MIR) and TIR measurements, where active combustion produces its strongest signal. Sensors such as MODIS and VIIRS provide real-time thermal anomaly detection, allowing early hotspot identification and assessment of burned areas.

The challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a calendar of burning activity based on active fire attack points, allowing emergency and early warning responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of ​​interest.

Our team went further and also addressed the need for both fire monitoring technicians and the Brigade members in charge of combating outbreaks, who are often unable to communicate, to be notified and communicated in the field of tasks through network communication devices with LoRa technology using open source applications called Meshtastic + ATAK. In this way, they can be aware of the outbreaks and the atmospheric conditions, in addition to being communicated through a secure network.

Objective

The goal was to develop a harmonized combustion activity calendar based on active fire hotspots in a web application,

The first thing that was done was the harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS hotspots, so that at the end of that phase the source sensor no longer matters and the patterns, trends and anomalies become the focus. The harmonization includes in the first stage the harmonization of the heat sources in the period in which both sensors overlap (but especially in the particular case of Carpinteria, which had 3 fires in that period). In a second stage, the FWI index is added to the first harmonization, achieving a robust formula

All this was based on the offers proposed by the challenge through the Nasa Fiirms and Meteomatic apps.

The second consisted of developing a web application that takes harmonized hotspot data as input.

In this case, a web application was developed with two tabs:

The first shows a map with heat sources, the user can select a region and a specific date range, then download analyzes and visualizations of fire activity as well as notifications of ongoing outbreaks.

The second web application would give emergency managers a view of fires in a given area

A calendar of combustion activity was created that shows the number of hotspots detected from the early 2000s to the present.

Downloadable CSV file of detected hot spots was created.

The pilot test was carried out on a location in the province of San Luis, called Carpintería (the tourist town located in the Junín Department, province of San Luis, Argentina) Latitude: 32° 24′ 00″ S (in decimal: -32.4°) Longitude: 65° 01′ 00″ W (in decimal: -65.01666667°) over a period of 20 years.

Specific variables were taken to harmonize the data, these were

Lat and long Geographic Coordinates

K-brightness

frp

Trust

FWI index

HIA (Harmonic Index of Focus)
